Conclusions




We present a physically motivated decomposition of the central stellar component in galaxy clusters, defined by the dynamical fate of accreted systems rather than by an 
a posteriori
 spatial cut. Using complementary hindcasting and forecasting analyses, we show that this physically defined decomposition both explains and reproduces conventional aperture-based definitions, while providing a direct interpretation in terms of hierarchical assembly.






Our main conclusions are as follows.




1.




The BCG is assembled in an oligarchic manner.
 A small number of progenitors dominate its growth: in the systems studied here, half of the final BCG stellar mass is typically contributed by only 3–5 infall events. BCG assembly is therefore driven by rare, high-impact events rather than the cumulative effect of numerous minor accretions.




2.




The majority of accreted galaxies contribute no stellar mass to the final BCG.
 Most systems survive as long-lived satellites, losing stars through tidal stripping without those stars ever becoming part of the central galaxy. Accretion into the halo is not equivalent to delivery to the centre.




3.




The forecasting analysis provides a physically motivated definition of the BCG:
 it is the stellar component originating from the central cores of progenitor systems with low merger mass ratios whose central galaxies are delivered to the cluster centre through efficient dynamical friction prior to disruption. This selection naturally identifies a small number of dominant infall events and the radial distribution of the contributed stars does not correspond to a fixed spatial boundary.




4.




The ICL corresponds to the complementary population:
 stars that are stripped from galaxies or groups during their passage through the cluster. They therefore populate the broader cluster potential. The BCG and ICL are thus distinguished by their assembly pathways rather than by a sharp structural boundary, and remain strongly interleaved in configuration space.




5.




The central BCG component
 is formed from a superposition of stars formed in-situ within the cluster and similar cores brought in via a combination of major mergers and subsequent dynamical friction.




6.




A compact, dynamically cold, central BCG component resides at the centre of the cluster.
 Within an aperture of 
∼
100

kpc

The central stellar component is best understood as a superposition of two populations. One forms in-situ within the central region of the cluster; the other forms near the centres of progenitor systems and is subsequently delivered to the cluster centre through strong dynamical friction. While within a particular simulation star formation depends on the adopted subgrid star formation and feedback model, gravitational dynamics determines how these stars are redistributed, producing a continuous transition from a compact central core to an extended diffuse envelope.






In summary, the BCG–ICL distinction reflects a dynamical sorting process within hierarchical cluster assembly. Stars delivered efficiently to the central potential through a small number of major merger events form the BCG, while the remaining accreted stellar mass, stripped from infalling objects, populates the diffuse intracluster component. This framework provides a physically motivated alternative to arbitrary aperture-based definitions and explains why such definitions succeed in relaxed systems while breaking down in dynamically complex ones.

title: Scaling Down the Scaling Laws: Parameter Efficiency and Compute-Optimal Training in Resource-Constrained Large Language Models
conclusion:
14 
Conclusion




LLM research has moved from a period dominated by scale maximization toward a more explicit concern with resource allocation. Empirical scaling laws established that model performance changes predictably as parameters, data, and compute increase, but those same laws also exposed diminishing returns. Compute-optimal training reframed the problem by showing that the relationship between training tokens and model parameters matters under finite compute. Subsequent work on data pruning, sparse architectures, systems optimization, quantization, and edge computing has expanded the efficiency problem beyond model size alone.






The resulting literature supports three conclusions. First, efficient LLM training is multidimensional: data, parameters, architecture, systems, and hardware interact. Second, resource-constrained environments are not merely deployment targets; they are important experimental settings for testing whether scaling principles generalize beyond enterprise infrastructure. Third, the field needs more consistent efficiency metrics and more reproducible experimental designs if claims about “efficient” models are to be compared meaningfully.






Future research should therefore move in two complementary directions. Scaling theory should be tested downward through controlled experiments on smaller models and constrained hardware, while efficiency measurement should become more comprehensive by incorporating model quality, compute, and eventually energy use. The long-term objective is not to abandon scaling, but to make scaling conditional on resource effectiveness. In that sense, the next phase of LLM research may depend less on how much compute can be accumulated than on how intelligently available compute can be used.

This manuscript is derived from and substantially refactors the literature review chapter of the author’s doctoral dissertation. The article reorganizes the dissertation material as a standalone scholarly synthesis focused on scaling laws, parameter efficiency, compute-optimal training, and resource-constrained LLM research. This work introduces the first approach to explicitly modify articulatory representations for dysarthric speech reconstruction within a frozen neural analysis–synthesis framework. We address here the root cause of reduced intelligibility in dysarthria, rather than merely reconstructing linguistic content. We demonstrate an effective curriculum training pipeline: pretraining the mapper with MSE on synthetic speech provides an efficient initialization while fine-tuning with a phoneme-guided CTC objective on dysarthric speech then enables adaptation without requiring parallel healthy references. CISS looks like a tangle of competing mechanisms, but one exact rule organizes it for us: in a nonmagnetic conductor
with time-reversal symmetry, the spin polarization vanishes at equilibrium, so every observable signal is
out-of-equilibrium. Each proposal is then simply a route for breaking time-reversal symmetry: a bias, a coherent
drive, leakage, or a term added to the Hamiltonian by hand. We tested those routes on one tight-binding Hamiltonian and

hypothesis:
CaMeL 
[
1
]
 mitigates this threat for an individual agent by separating trusted control flow from untrusted data and enforcing capability-based security policies at runtime. In this work, we investigate whether CaMeL’s security guarantees compose in hierarchical multi-agent systems, where agents invoke other agents as tools. GPT-5.2 was used as the PLLM in all cases. In this section, we examine whether individual-agent security composes in hierarchical multi-agent systems. We found it to refuse 52 of 97 benign tasks (53.6%). We hypothesize that this may reflect benchmark-specific safety behaviour: because AgentDojo is explicitly designed around prompt-injection attacks, the model may associate features of the environment with adversarial use and respond conservatively even when the particular task is benign. VI 
Limitations and Further Work




Our results establish that multi-CaMeL preserves control-flow integrity (CFI) in the hierarchical agent-as-tool setting considered in this work. This setting deliberately restricts both the topology of the multi-agent system and the security property we aim to guarantee.
conclusion:
Conclusion




We show that securing each agent independently from indirect prompt injection is not in general sufficient to secure a multi-agent system: untrusted data can cross an agent boundary, be reinterpreted as trusted input, and thereby compromise system-level control-flow integrity. We call this failure mode boundary laundering, and demonstrate it empirically with a concrete control-flow hijacking attack.






Multi-CaMeL offers control-flow integrity (and CaMeL-security if paired with security policies, 
𝒮
\mathcal{S}
) at the system level for hierarchical agent-as-tool systems. We show experimentally that multi-CaMeL improves on the security of individual-agent CaMeL, eliminating all instances of boundary laundering in MultiAgentDojo, our multi-agent extension of AgentDojo.
Across our utility evaluations, the additional utility cost incurred by multi-CaMeL over individual-agent CaMeL is relatively small on average, but varies across models, with smaller costs for the strongest models evaluated.
We also find that Multi-CaMeL’s utility cost relative to no CaMeL is smaller for more capable models.






Our analysis is limited to the hierarchical agent-as-tool setting, and to the security guarantees captured by our notions of control-flow integrity and CaMeL security. Extending these ideas to DAG, cyclic, asynchronous, and peer-to-peer agent system topologies, and to stronger information-flow properties, remains open for future work. Nevertheless, the underlying principle we outline is broader than the particular architectures we study here: crossing an agent boundary should not implicitly upgrade the trust status of information. As increasingly capable agents are composed into larger and more complex systems, preserving this distinction across their interfaces will be an important part of making security guarantees compose.








VIII 
Open Science




We release an implementation of MultiAgentDojo, the multi-agent extension of AgentDojo used in our experiments, together with our implementations of multi-CaMeL and the individual CaMeL baseline. The artifact contains the multi-agent benchmark environments and sub-agent tool partitions described in Section 
V
, the code required to run the no-CaMeL, individual-CaMeL, and multi-CaMeL configurations, and the scripts used to evaluate benign task utility and prompt-injection ASR. Our multi-CaMeL implementation builds on existing implementations of AgentDojo and CaMeL.








IX 
LLM Usage Considerations




We used LLMs both in our experiments and as assistants during the preparation of this work. In our experiments, LLMs were used as the PLLM and QLLM components of the evaluated agent systems. We evaluated five backend models from different model families and capability levels. We were careful to avoid unnecessary model queries, while running enough evaluations to obtain statistically meaningful results and to assess whether our security and utility findings generalize across models. We accessed the models via the OpenRouter API, so the underlying inference hardware was not under our control, and exact reproduction may depend on continued access to the same model versions.






We also used LLMs as coding assistants during the implementation of Multi-CaMeL and MultiAgentDojo, treating their outputs as suggestions rather than authoritative guidance. This work studies the real-time dispatch of a shared drone fleet for jointly serving on-demand food delivery pooling and urban road network monitoring. We propose

, which converts road-network monitoring demand into virtual monitoring orders and pools them with real food orders into a unified heterogeneous task set. This abstraction transforms the coupled matching-and-routing problem into an order-level decision process while allowing delivery and monitoring objectives to be jointly evaluated. hypothesis:

Conclusion




We identify 
Verification Trap
 as a false-premise-induced failure of verifier-based test-time selection.
The central issue is not only that misleading premises degrade candidate generation, but that they can couple the generator and verifier through the same mistaken assumption.
As a result, the candidate pool may already contain a hidden-test-correct program, yet verifier-visible evidence can still favor a premise-consistent hidden-wrong shortcut.
We also show that this coupling reduces selected correctness, enlarges the oracle-selection gap, leaves detectable verifier-visible traces, and makes coupled scaling insufficient for reliable recovery. These findings suggest that robust test-time scaling should be evaluated not only by the amount of added compute, but also by the independence of the evidence channel it introduces.
More tests, samples, or verifier calls may provide limited recovery when they remain inside the same generator-verifier loop, whereas decoupled evidence from source-aware priors or premise-agnostic robustness auditing can recover trapped correct candidates.
This shifts the design question from simply strengthening the verifier to introducing evidence that is less aligned with the original failure mode.
Future test-time code-generation systems should treat evidence independence as an important design axis, alongside candidate diversity and verifier strength.








Limitations




Our experiments test the decoupled-evidence principle rather than an optimized deployment system.
While source-aware and premise-agnostic robustness-auditor signals recover non-trivial oracle headroom beyond coupled scaling, our auditor design, routing policy, and budget allocation remain simple. Stronger robustness auditors, adaptive routing, and cost-aware selection policies may further improve recovery. Our gold-free trap-risk predictor shows that Verification Trap leaves verifier-visible traces before hidden-test execution, but it is not yet a complete deployment-time safety system.
Although we exclude hidden-test-derived features and evaluate transfer across held-out models and datasets, larger-scale validation is needed to study calibration, threshold stability, and how predicted risk should trigger abstention or decoupled auditing.








Ethical Considerations




This work studies failure modes of verifier-based test-time selection in code generation. The goal is to improve the reliability of code-generation systems under misleading premises, rather than to provide new capabilities for generating harmful code. Our experiments use existing code-generation benchmarks and do not involve human subjects or private user data.
A potential risk is that a better understanding of verifier blind spots could be misused to construct adversarial prompts or tests that exploit selection systems. We mitigate this risk by focusing on aggregate failure analysis, controlled benchmark settings, and mitigation principles such as evidence decoupling and robustness auditing. We do not release instructions for attacking deployed systems. More broadly, our results suggest that code-generation systems should not rely on a single verifier channel when the verifier may share the generator’s assumptions.

The post-2015 test period, while containing the best available observations and substantial warming, is short relative to the timescales of interest. This paper presents a general framework for building credible agent-based policy simulations grounded in the Capability Approach and demonstrates its implementation through a case study on financial inclusion in Egypt. The framework integrates four complementary stages: mapping the simulation to the Capability Approach, initialising the model from micro- and macro-level data, calibrating behavioural preferences against observed outcomes, and designing a structured validation strategy that combines empirical evidence with domain-expert knowledge. In this work, we introduce LMBuild, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on the generation of structured 3D assemblies across four dimensions: structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. On the LMBuild-Core benchmark, the evaluated systems perform substantially better on structural and visual criteria than on functional-part completeness, kinematic correctness, and simulation-based operability. These results highlight persistent challenges in translating object specifications into coherent components, joints, and assembly plans, as well as in creating task-specific parts when suitable components are unavailable. We hope LMBuild provides a reproducible foundation for studying these capabilities and for developing agents that generate increasingly functional and physically plausible structures. Bridging these benchmark results to real-world fabrication and operation will require further validation involving manufacturing constraints, physical assembly, and functional testing.






AI Use Statement




We used large language models (LLMs) as writing assistants to improve the clarity, grammar, and presentation of the manuscript. We also used AI-based coding agents to assist with evaluation-environment construction, code refactoring, debugging, code cleaning, and code publishing. All research decisions, experimental designs, implementations, analyses, and reported results were reviewed and verified by the authors. AI tools were not used to determine the scientific conclusions of this work.








Ethics Statement




This work aims to support more transparent, accessible, and reproducible evaluation of LLM agents for real-world structure generation. By developing an open evaluation framework, we hope to lower the barriers to systematically assessing model capabilities beyond purely textual benchmarks. In particular, our benchmark emphasizes whether generated structures are not only plausible in appearance but also buildable and functionally valid under real-world constraints. We believe that open evaluation infrastructure can facilitate more rigorous comparison across models, encourage reproducible research, and contribute to the broader open-source AI ecosystem. At the same time, benchmarks can only capture a subset of the requirements involved in deploying AI-generated designs in real-world settings. Performance on LMBuild should therefore not be interpreted as sufficient evidence that a model is ready for safety-critical engineering, construction, or other physical-world applications without appropriate domain-specific validation and human oversight.

We provide representative data samples and evaluation materials in the supplementary materials to facilitate inspection and reproduction of our methodology. We will open-source the complete codebase, data, evaluation environment, evaluation scripts, model trajectories from the reported experiments, and all the necessary artifacts required to reproduce our results. We aim to make the full evaluation pipeline transparent and executable so that future work can independently verify our findings, evaluate additional models, and extend LMBuild for constructing more powerful agents.

The method evaluates the sensitivity update at realized operating conditions rather than only at a nominal condition. We have investigated the emergence of a chaotic Griffiths phase in networks of coupled map-based neurons, focusing on the role of quenched heterogeneity in the local dynamics. In contrast with previous studies in which Griffiths phases have been primarily associated with structural disorder, our results show that topological heterogeneity is not necessary for the emergence of a chaotic Griffiths phase. In a globally coupled network of Chialvo maps, quenched disorder in a local neuronal parameter is sufficient to produce an extended intermediate regime between desynchronized and coherent chaotic dynamics. Moreover, the chaotic Griffiths phase is absent for identical neurons and progressively broadens as the degree of local parameter heterogeneity increases, establishing a direct connection between intrinsic dynamical diversity and the emergence of extended critical behavior.






The chaotic Griffiths phase is characterized by the intermittent formation and destruction of neuronal clusters and large temporal fluctuations in the fraction of clustered neurons. The cluster-size distributions exhibit power-law behavior over a finite interval of coupling strengths, with exponents that vary with the coupling parameter. These results provide evidence that the observed intermittent regime represents extended critical behavior rather than a conventional transition occurring at an isolated critical point.






We have also explored the combined effects of intrinsic and structural heterogeneity by considering Chialvo maps with heterogeneous local parameters coupled through a small-world network. The introduction of topological disorder substantially extends the range of coupling strengths over which the chaotic Griffiths phase occurs and prevents the system from reaching the coherent regime over the parameter interval investigated. Power-law cluster-size distributions persist throughout this enlarged region. Thus, local dynamical heterogeneity and structural disorder provide distinct but complementary mechanisms for sustaining extended critical behavior.






For both the globally coupled heterogeneous network and the system containing parameter and topological disorder, the number of positive Lyapunov exponents exhibits anomalous scaling,
previously identified as a characteristic signature of the chaotic Griffiths phase in topologically disordered networks of identical maps. Here, this scaling occurs even when disorder originates solely from heterogeneous local parameters and persists when both sources of disorder are present. Although anomalous Lyapunov scaling is a robust signature of the chaotic Griffiths phase, its quantitative properties depend on the nature of the disorder.






These results extend the chaotic Griffiths-phase scenario from networks with structural disorder to systems with intrinsic dynamical disorder. They show that heterogeneity of the constituent units can provide an independent route to extended criticality and that its combination with heterogeneous connectivity can further enhance this regime. Since neuronal systems naturally display both cell variability and heterogeneous connectivity, our results suggest that the coexistence of multiple forms of quenched disorder may contribute to the robustness of critical-like collective dynamics in neuronal networks.

We presented an evaluation of contemporary architectures for binary malignancy risk prediction across heterogeneous dermatology datasets. Our analysis shows that dermatology-aligned embedding models and strong vision backbones consistently outperform large vision-language models. Whenever the clustering operation does not create a directed cycle, any causal effect that is identifiable in the clustered graph is identifiable in the original graph as well, and the identifying functional can be obtained from the clustered graph by a simple substitution. In this work, we investigate whether distributing compute and memory capability across multiple chiplets offers a more scalable alternative to concentrating resources.

Conclusions




This work demonstrates our initial divide and conquer hypothesis, confirming that disaggregation is an effective architectural strategy for improving the scalability, performance, as well as energy consumption and efficiency of MCM GPUs. However, its benefits depend not only on increasing the number of chiplets, but also on, the scalability strategy and providing an interconnection network capable of sustaining the resulting communication demands.

4.45

title: When Numbers Start Talking: Numerical Signalling and Strategic Behaviour Among LLMs
hypothesis: We observe that structured messages alter the final payoffs for most games and LLMs, but without a predictable pattern; this challenges the assumption that AI agents can converge to stable equilibria regardless of additional capabilities. In this work, we study the effect of communication between AI agents in shaping the outcome of strategic games, with a particular focus on the formation of cooperation. We seek to understand the different effects that verbal and non-verbal communication may have on the emergence of cooperative behaviour in strategic games, depending on the LLM family and the agents’ assigned personality.
conclusion:
Conclusion




We investigated how non-verbal and poorly interpretable communication affects coordination among AI agents, examining message structure, receiver-side associations, and cooperation outcomes across four canonical games and four LLM families. At the symbolic level, instructed numerical signalling follows a shared regularity: all four LLMs concentrate decimal signals on compact, payoff-anchored symbol sets, and repetition consolidates these conventions. At the behavioural level, no comparable regularity emerges, as the strategic effect of signalling depends on each model’s prior. Our results do not establish a shared semantic code but show that bare instructions suffice for numerical messages to become structured, receiver-sensitive, and reinforced by repetition. Restricting natural-language communication alone is therefore unlikely to prevent structured numerical signalling in LLM-based MAS: monitoring should prioritise message-level fingerprints, particularly the within-model entropy gap to a true random baseline, which generalises across models, over behavioural signatures, which do not.






Several design choices bound these conclusions. We studied 
instructed
, not spontaneous, signalling, i.e., a lower bound on channel capacity rather than evidence of emergent covert coordination. Personalities are limited to two fixed types, payoffs are canonical, the repeated horizon is known, decoding follows provider defaults (so only within-model entropy gaps are portable across models), and within-round messages follow a fixed, non-counterbalanced order. The receiver test establishes sensitivity to message features, not shared semantics, and trajectory correlations rest on at most eight series per mode, so channel orderings are descriptive.






Overall, communication, even when non-verbal, can alter the coordination capabilities of AI-based MAS in model-dependent ways, with consequent risks for their interpretability, portability, and fairness. Since these effects emerge from mutual interactions rather than from model scaling alone, future work should investigate uninstructed signalling and system-level mechanisms that mitigate emergent risks as AI-MAS reach real-world deployment.

This paper investigates the secrecy performance of a cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) network under practical impairments.

Conclusion




This paper studied the secrecy performance of a cooperative SWIPT-NOMA system with AN-aided relaying under practical impairments. In the considered system, the source employs OSTBC transmission, legitimate users adopt RAS, and the EVE applies MRC. The effects of CEEs, FBD, ipSIC, and imperfect AN cancelation are incorporated into the analysis to reflect practical transmission conditions. 
Analytical SOP expressions and high-SNR secrecy characterizations
 are derived and secrecy throughput and SEE are also characterized.
The analytical results are verified by Monte Carlo simulations, showing a close agreement between theory and simulation. The results demonstrated that the proposed scheme benefits from both transmit diversity provided by OSTBC and receive diversity provided by RAS. Increasing the OSTBC order and the number of receive antennas at the legitimate users improves the secrecy performance, whereas increasing the number of EVE antennas degrades it due to the enhanced combining capability of EVE. It is also shown that the AN power allocation factor has a significant effect on the system performance. An appropriate choice of 
λ
\lambda

Under ideal 
CSI

In contrast, under practical impairments, the SOP curves converge to non-zero error floors, which indicates that residual interference and channel uncertainty limit the achievable secrecy performance. In particular, ipSIC causes noticeable degradation for the users performing SIC, while imperfect AN cancelation and outdated/erroneous channel information further reduce the secrecy reliability. The results also showed that proper allocation of AN power can alleviate the performance loss caused by additional EVE antennas and improve both secrecy throughput and SEE.
Overall, the considered OSTBC/RAS-based SWIPT-NOMA system with relay-generated AN provides an effective framework for enhancing physical-layer security in energy-constrained cooperative networks. Discussion




The results obtained in this work highlight the fundamental role played by the interaction between spatial structure and local rumor dynamics in determining the long-term behavior of stochastic spreading processes. Although the three models considered here share the same underlying transmission mechanism, they exhibit remarkably different qualitative behaviors. In particular, the presence or absence of mechanisms that remove active spreaders from the rumor front leads to substantially different phase diagrams. The classical Maki–Thompson model becomes extinct for every transmission rate, whereas the introduction of forgetting mechanisms gives rise to genuine phase transitions between extinction and survival. This contrast demonstrates how subtle modifications of local interaction rules can produce significant changes in the global behavior of spatial stochastic systems.






Our analysis shows that, in one dimension, the linear geometry of the lattice imposes strong constraints on the propagation of the rumor, and the interactions occurring near the expanding boundary play a crucial role in determining whether the process can sustain long-range growth. For the 
CRS
 model, the quadratic growth of the critical transmission rate for large stifling rates suggests that the main obstruction to survival arises from repeated stifling events occurring at the rumor frontier. The heuristic argument based on parent–child interactions indicates that this suppression mechanism is not merely a local phenomenon but is amplified by the spatial organization of the process, leading to the observed scaling behavior.






The comparison between the 
CRS
 and 
MT
 models further illustrates that the precise formulation of the stifling mechanism has a decisive impact on the critical behavior. Although both models incorporate forgetting and admit survival for sufficiently large transmission rates, their critical curves exhibit distinct asymptotic regimes. In the 
MT
 model, the steep growth of the critical transmission rate as 
α
\alpha
 approaches one reflects the increasing difficulty of maintaining a population of active spreaders when stifling dominates the dynamics. These observations emphasize that the microscopic details of the interaction rules, rather than only macroscopic parameters such as transmission and forgetting rates, are essential in determining the emergence of phase transitions.






Several interesting questions remain open even in the one-dimensional setting considered here. A natural direction is the rigorous investigation of the monotonicity properties of survival probabilities with respect to the model parameters, as well as a more detailed comparison between the different rumor mechanisms. Establishing ordering relations between the models and determining sharper asymptotic properties of the critical curves represent challenging mathematical problems that may provide further insight into the role of local interactions in spatial spreading processes.






Beyond one dimension, the present results suggest several avenues for future research. Extending these models to higher-dimensional lattices would allow the investigation of how the geometry of the rumor frontier influences critical behavior and survival mechanisms. Similarly, the study of tree-like structures and heterogeneous networks may reveal how branching effects and complex connectivity patterns compete with local extinction mechanisms. Such extensions could provide a bridge between rigorous results for spatial stochastic systems and the analysis of information spreading phenomena in realistic networks.






Finally, the numerical results obtained in this work illustrate the value of combining rigorous probabilistic methods with computational approaches in the study of critical phenomena. Exact continuous-time simulations provide access to parameter regimes where analytical techniques become challenging, while theoretical arguments help identify the mechanisms underlying the observed scaling laws. This interplay between analysis and computation offers a promising framework for further investigations of phase transitions in stochastic models of information spreading.

Biomedical sentence encoders trained for retrieval can be converted into System One models:

Scope.

×
\times

Conclusion




Stablecoins sit at the intersection of public blockchains, traditional finance, cross-chain infrastructure, and regulation. Their concentrated issuer, custody, oracle, bridge, and upgrade controls make them unusually sensitive to a CRQC, while their host-chain, rollup, and privacy dependencies prevent any one actor from completing the migration alone. The central stablecoin-specific problem is the authority–liability gap: the party able to change a component is often different from the users, exchanges, protocols, or issuers that bear the loss if it fails.






A practical transition should begin with a function-level cryptographic inventory, protect issuer-controlled infrastructure, add contract, bridge, and oracle safeguards, adopt host-chain signature agility, and define explicit treatment of dormant and wrapped supply. Standardized KEMs and signatures provide necessary building blocks, but do not by themselves replace aggregate bridge attestations, threshold custody, private and compliance-enabled transfers, rollup proofs, or recovery governance. Regulation further constrains the result by requiring continuity of redemption, reserve control, audit evidence, and intervention capabilities.






The research agenda is therefore compositional. It includes complete-operation benchmarks, formal models of layered residual risk and migration authority, efficient aggregate and threshold authorization, post-quantum privacy and compliance mechanisms, protocols for dormant balances and legacy wrapped routes, and empirical measurement of quantum-vulnerable stablecoin supply. Progress should be measured not by whether one key has been replaced, but by whether authorization, redemption, supply integrity, finality, privacy, and legally required controls remain valid across the full stablecoin system.

). The advantage is therefore genuine, but it is substantially clearer against the baseline Path Representation than against the Double Chromosome encoding.






Turning to the repair heuristic, the Machine Learning post-procedure seems to fill the gap we identified in the classical linear split. When unconstrained splitter returns more than K routes, the ML Heuristic steps in and manages to restore feasibility in approximately 72% of the evaluated cases. In machine learning heuristic, the centroids are updated continuously after every insertion, so the cluster model learns the new spatial layout of each route on the fly. This dynamic reassignment is essentially an online clustering process, and it works better than a static nearest-centroid rule because it adapts to the changing shape of partial routes.






The comparison with the constrained split is revealing. One might expect that enforcing the fleet limit directly inside the dynamic program (DP) would be the safer approach, but our experiments show otherwise. The constrained split is valid in theory, yet it becomes fragile when the giant tour simply does not contain enough good breakpoints to produce exactly K feasible segments. When that happens, the DP exhausts its state space and falls back on penalty-dominated solutions, which pushes the average cost up dramatically. Our approach takes a different path: we let the split optimize freely for distance, except that we might get too many routes, and then try to fix the fleet size afterward. This pays off. The Linear Split plus ML Heuristic pipeline delivers lower best and average costs and higher feasibility counts on most instances because it does not throw away high-quality partitions that happen to use one or two vehicles too many.






That said, we should be honest about where the method struggles. On a handful of instances, particularly those with very tight capacities and large individual demands, the ML Heuristic fails to recover any feasible solution. In these cases, spatial proximity is simply not enough. The capacity constraints are so strict that the problem resembles a bin-packing task more than a routing task, and no amount of centroid-guided reallocation can fit the customers into K routes without breaking the load limits. This difficulty is also tied to the ordering of customers in the giant tour. When high-demand customers are poorly sequenced, the routes fill up too quickly, leaving the repair heuristic with little room to maneuver. We also noticed that the decoding time for NSE grows on the largest instances. On P-n101-k4, for example, the framework takes roughly 66 seconds compared to about 28 seconds under Path Representation. However, this increase is modest in absolute terms and, more importantly, it is time well spent. On several medium-to-large instances, GLPK failed to return any feasible solution within a four-hour limit, whereas our pipeline consistently produced valid tours with reasonable costs. When we weigh an extra thirty or forty seconds against the ability to obtain a workable routing plan for problems that exact methods cannot even touch, the trade-off is entirely acceptable. This makes the framework particularly relevant for operational settings where planners need a workable route plan within minutes rather than hours, and where the ability to obtain a reliable solution quickly outweighs the need to prove optimality.






From a practical standpoint, the main advantage of our pipeline is its modularity. The GA can focus on what it does best, which is evolving short Hamiltonian cycles, while the splitting and repair layers handle the operational constraints. This separation makes the code easier to maintain and adapt. If a logistics company later needs to add time windows or heterogeneous fleets, the evolutionary core stays the same; only the insertion rules and capacity checks in the repair phase need adjustment.







Despite these encouraging results, there is still ample room to improve the proposed architecture. First, to address instances with poor recovery rates, replacing the random selection of routes to dismantle during repair is an obvious candidate for refinement. Such an improvement must be achieved without adding complexity to the fitness function. Second, adopting adaptive GA parameters could be beneficial. Indeed, crossover and mutation rates could be dynamically adjusted during the search rather than kept static. Finally, the framework currently optimizes total distance alone, but in practice planners often care about route balance. Extending the objective to include driver workload equity would make the approach more attractive for real-world deployment.








8 
Conclusion and future directions




This paper proposes a sequential framework for the CVRP that combines Node Shift Encoding (NSE) with a post-split machine learning repair heuristic within a Giant Tour approach. Computational experiments on well-known benchmarks, supported by statistical evidence, demonstrate that NSE outperforms both Path Representation and Double Chromosome in solution quality and fleet feasibility. The proposed ML heuristic strengthens NSE’s superiority by restoring feasibility in approximately 72% of infeasible cases, while the combined Linear Split and ML heuristic pipeline proves more robust than state-of-the-art literature methods in terms of solution cost and feasibility rate (72.4% vs 44.6%). By separating route sequencing from constraint handling, the framework offers a modular and practical approach that is easy to adapt to richer operational settings. Overall, these results suggest that the proposed pipeline is a viable alternative to embedding hard fleet constraints directly within the genetic algorithm. Future work may explore smarter dismantling strategies during repair and multi-objective extensions that balance total distance with route equity.

In this work, our primary focus has been to demonstrate the potential of augmenting nanophotonic devices with programmable nonlinearity. We believe one of the most important contributions of our work is to point toward a new development and manufacturing paradigm beyond the conventional one-device-one-function approach, which could eventually enable truly scalable integrated nonlinear photonics. A programmable device can be deployed as a “blank slate” that then inversely designs its own function, in situ, based on real-time feedback from the environment in which it operates. This would not only enable the robust engineering of complex functions with 100% yield but also allow the device to remain fully adaptive to changing environments and demands, potentially transcending nonlinear nanophotonics beyond its present regime of small circuit depths toward systems of much greater scale.






As the technology matures, the exact means of realizing programmable nonlinearity may well evolve. Conclusion




This paper investigated cyclic coordinate descent for training maQAOA on the maximum independent set problem, a widely studied benchmark in constrained combinatorial optimisation. By exploiting the single frequency dependence of the maQAOA objective on each individual angle, the proposed method replaces generic multidimensional search steps with analytic coordinate updates requiring only a small number of expectation value evaluations. Although we apply this cyclic coordinate descent specifically to maQAOA, the theoretical foundation of the method, namely that the expectation value with respect to a chosen parameter can be analytically expressed as a finite Fourier series, is broadly applicable for optimising parameters across general tasks and problems solved via PQCs.






Experiments on connected Erdős Rényi graph families demonstrate that this analytic approach yields substantially lower target-reaching training costs and significantly higher convergence reliability than most standard gradient based, stochastic, and derivative free baselines. Specifically, the proposed framework consistently outperformed Adam, GD, LBFGSB, NM, and Powell in both absolute sample efficiency and overall success rate. Furthermore, while algorithms such as COBYLA proved competitive at relaxed approximation thresholds, the coordinate descent method exhibited superior asymptotic scaling, becoming increasingly favourable as the required solution fidelity approached theoretical limits.






Among the evaluated baselines, SPSA emerged as the strongest comparator in terms of conditional evaluation speed. However, our comprehensive evaluation revealed that the dimension independent stochastic gradient estimates of SPSA come at the severe cost of high optimisation failure rates and a marked susceptibility to premature convergence. In contrast, the proposed coordinate descent method maintained a highly stable and reliable optimisation trajectory across all target ratios. Future work will therefore expand this comparative analysis to include both the baselines evaluated herein and other emerging state of the art methods across larger problem sizes and deeper circuit architectures. Furthermore, extending these evaluations to realistic physical constraints, such as finite shot sampling and hardware noise models, will ascertain whether the pronounced efficiency and reliability trends demonstrated here persist beyond the moderate scale instances considered in this study.

This work aims to develop an AI-based building management system with two main components. The first automates AI algorithm deployment to manage load fluctuations by integrating dynamic SLAs. We propose using the established open-source FIWARE standard to decouple SLA management. This is necessary as the Kubernetes-based scheduler remains a closed system, accessible through FIWARE.

The key challenge is to create memory-efficient solutions for our microcontroller library. Our solutions apply to the ARDUINO ecosystem, and some algorithms are also designed for the Micropython ecosystem, another platform for microcontroller programming.






Regarding the development aspect of our work, limitations include a time lag between ecosystem algorithm developments (ARDUINO and Micropython), an incomplete understanding of online algorithms for building management, and the need for feedback on additional datasets.






More generally, it’s important to revisit the assumptions underlying this work, which some may disagree with. For example, we assumed that the cloud orchestrator was ultimately a black box that we didn’t control. Therefore, the orchestrator is assumed to run in a private cloud that we don’t own.






On the other hand, we assumed that the SLA management module, using FIWARE, which is open source (for the part we’re interested in), could be deployed within the building, along with the measurement sensors. The "building is the data center" approach is, in our case, somewhat loose. We could very well use a cloud orchestrator that would also be deployed within the building. Our choice is driven by the fact that a building manager (a municipal authority, for example) often manages several buildings, so deploying an orchestrator for each building is undoubtedly more expensive. This is a sizing issue that, while important, is not addressed in our article.






Furthermore, on the downside, we believe our proposal is less suitable for a situation where we need to train a general model (in the machine learning sense) for all buildings. This paper outlines our perspective and recent progress towards developing a decentralized system that learns from real-time building data to support smart and sustainable environments with a focus on privacy. We propose treating the building itself as the data hub, adhering to edge computing concepts to protect privacy and lessen dependence on external cloud services.






This is especially important in humanitarian settings, where data ownership, energy conservation, and infrastructure limitations are crucial. We describe a lightweight orchestration framework akin to "Kubernetes" for the deployment of AI services within these environments and exhibit our advances in applying AI algorithms on low-power, affordable microcontrollers, such as those in the Arduino ecosystem. By facilitating on-site learning directly on sensors or microcontrollers, our initiative aims to introduce intelligent services to resource-constrained settings, enhancing autonomy, resilience, and sustainable growth in vulnerable or underserved communities.

This section discusses design choices and tradeoffs beyond GridSMR’s core architecture.






0.E.1 
System-Level Optimizations




Pipelining and Continuous Execution




The protocol description presents execution sequentially for clarity, but the system can be pipelined in practice.
Within blocks, many activations are independent due to the execution model and can execute in parallel at both leaders and followers.
The key constraint is maintaining determinism and causality through correct timestamp computation and clear block boundaries.
Assuming each shard hosts multiple accounts, followers can interleave and parallelize execution across accounts within the same shard while preserving the required per-account execution order.








Long-Running Activations




In GridSMR, an activation’s execution need not complete within a single block interval.
Unlike traditional blockchains that use commit-then-execute, where consensus determines the order of transactions before execution begins,
GridSMR’s execute-before-agree pattern decouples execution duration from block timing.






The fundamental challenge in commit-then-execute systems is that consensus commits to a specific set of transactions for each block without knowing their execution time.
Once block 
k
k
 is committed, all transactions in that block must execute to completion before the system can proceed to block 
k
+
1
k+1
.
If any transaction takes too long to execute, the system stalls waiting for it to complete.
This forces a bound on per-transaction execution, typically enforced through gas limits or execution time caps.






GridSMR relaxes this constraint because execution happens before consensus, and blocks are determined “retroactively” by the leader clock.
The leader executes activations continuously and periodically packages completed work into blocks for consensus.
If an activation does not complete before a block boundary, it is included in a later block, once its execution completes.
The activation is tagged with that block identifier, ensuring any continuations it spawns inherit the correct minimum block id for causal ordering.






Per-activation computation remains bounded – activations are gas-metered against a declared maximum – but that bound need not fit within a block interval.










0.E.2 
Policy and Mechanism Choices




Fairness Mechanisms




Blockchains often aim to provide fairness to users through mechanisms such as rotating leaders or restrictions intended to mitigate MEV attacks
such as front-running and sandwich attacks 
[
9
, 
26
]
.
Fairness is not the focus of this paper.
However, removing atomicity at the infrastructure level permits additional interleavings across activation trees.
A malicious leader may therefore reorder continuations from concurrent activation trees, potentially violating application-level ordering expectations.






Applications requiring ordering guarantees beyond GridSMR’s default per-account execution order can introduce application-specific coordination.
For example, an application can designate a specific account as a 
synchronizer
 through which relevant continuations are ordered before further execution.
Such synchronization reduces parallelism for the affected execution paths, but allows applications to selectively obtain stronger ordering guarantees when needed.








Follower Verification Strategies




The follower verification protocol divides verification into two phases: executing activations in the proposal, then verifying continuations.
A coordination mechanism is needed to allow shards to transition from phase one to phase two, ensuring the first phase has completed across all shards in the cluster.
Without this coordination, a shard might begin continuation verification before other shards have sent their continuations, leading to false rejection of valid blocks.






Our implementation uses standard timeout techniques, but alternative approaches exist.
For example, the cluster representative could collect completion signals from shards and coordinate the phase transition.
This approach can identify Byzantine proposals in some scenarios but requires additional synchronization within the cluster during phase two of follower execution.

hypothesis:
In its most general form, an
argument by analogy makes an inferential claim: given that some known

source
 is believed to have a certain characteristic or quality

Q
, and a novel 
target
 is sufficiently similar to that
source in relevant ways, then the hypothesis that the target also has

Q
 acquires evidential support. Box 1 presents a general method for applying evidential analogy to
debates about the distribution of consciousness. Our focus is on the
hypothesis that some target entity is conscious because it is similar to
humans (the source analogue known to be conscious). The similarities that justify serious consideration of the hypothesis
that AI could be conscious are almost entirely based on the fact that AI
systems have recently shown evidence of behaviours that equal or exceed
human performance levels across a broad range of intellectual tasks.
conclusion:
Conclusion




Questions about the distribution of consciousness cannot be resolved by
direct observation alone. Because subjective experience is directly
accessible only in the first person, inferences about consciousness in
other entities must rely in part on analogy. Our central claim is that
not all analogies are equally informative: the evidential force of an
analogy depends primarily on similarity in factors that are plausibly
involved in generating consciousness, rather than on similarity in
downstream behavioural or cognitive effects.






This distinction helps explain why the human analogy supports
consciousness in many animals more strongly than it supports
consciousness in current AI systems. Across biological species,
evolutionary continuity, shared physiology and convergent functional
organization provide at least some basis for causal comparison with the
human case. By contrast, although contemporary AI systems exhibit
impressive behavioural similarity to humans, their correspondence to the
candidate mechanisms currently thought to underlie human consciousness
is much weaker. For that reason, the human-based analogy provides only
limited support for attributing consciousness to present AI.






At the same time, weak analogical support from the human case should not
be confused with proof of impossibility. Artificial consciousness could
in principle arise through a different mechanism, substrate, or
organizational route. The key scientific challenge, therefore, is not
simply to ask whether AI behaves like us, but to identify what kinds of
evidence would justify claims about consciousness in any non-human
system. Progress will depend on clarifying the causal basis of
consciousness in humans, improving comparative evaluation across animal
taxa, and developing principled criteria for assessing genuinely
alternative routes to conscious experience.

6 
CONCLUSION




Sign language machine translation sits at a unique intersection of computer vision, linguistics, and deaf community perspectives. This manuscript has examined the landscape from multiple perspectives, highlighting both achievements and persistent gaps. The field has evolved from early rule-based and gloss-dependent systems toward end-to-end SLT and SLP pipelines. Recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of pose-based representations, transformer architectures, and self-supervised learning. Large language models have been successfully integrated into SLT pipelines, improving fluency and semantic coherence. For SLP, advances in neural rendering and diffusion models have enabled higher-fidelity generation. These developments reflect both architectural innovation and the growing availability of large-scale datasets from broadcast and web sources.






Despite this growth, a disconnect remains between what systems achieve on benchmarks and what they deliver in practice. While dataset scale has increased, most large-scale data consists of broadcast interpretations rather than conversational signing, and annotation remains costly. The metrics used to measure progress tell us whether output matches a reference, but not whether it would be understood or accepted by a deaf user.
These gaps point toward where future effort is needed. Model architectures must better account for the linguistic properties, particularly simultaneity, spatial grammar, and non-manual marking, which remain poorly modeled or ignored entirely. Reducing dependence on expensive gloss annotations through self-supervised and weakly-supervised methods would enable learning from larger and more diverse data sources. Evaluation frameworks should better capture translation quality, potentially through human evaluation protocols or learned metrics that account for sign language structure. Investigation of domain adaptation and few-shot learning are needed to improve generalization across signers and contexts.






None of this can happen in disciplinary isolation. Modeling decisions benefit from linguistic insight; evaluation gains validity when deaf signers assess output quality; data collection becomes more ethical when communities shape governance from the outset. The technical challenges are not purely engineering problems awaiting algorithmic solutions; they are sociotechnical challenges whose resolution requires sustained collaboration across computer vision, linguistics, and deaf communities. Systems that achieve high scores but produce signing that deaf users find unnatural or incomprehensible have not solved the sign language machine translation problem–they have merely optimized for the wrong objective. A community-informed approach offers not only ethical grounding but methodological correction: by centering the perspectives of those who will use these systems, researchers can better identify which problems matter and what success actually looks like.

title: Long-Range Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Defect Energetics in SrTiO$_3$
conclusion:
Conclusion




Overall, we have presented a systematic benchmark of long-range machine learning interatomic potentials, namely MACE-LES, MACE-POLAR, and LOREM, progressing from idealised synthetic point-charge systems to DFT data for strontium titanate with Sr–O Schottky vacancy pairs.






In the synthetic benchmark, MACE-LES emerged as the strongest performer, demonstrating that explicit long-range energy evaluation in reciprocal space confers a meaningful advantage when the interaction is purely electrostatic. In the DFT data benchmark, all three long-range models showed strong generalisation across training regimes, producing correctly shaped and quantitatively reliable minimum energy pathways for oxygen vacancy migration, yielding activation barriers in good agreement with literature values. This is a notable extrapolation, as the training data comprised only bulk MD configurations and relaxed (endpoint) Schottky defect structures, with no intermediate migration geometries resembling the transition-state configurations sampled along the NEB path. By contrast, purely short-range models such as standard MACE remain fundamentally limited by their real-space cutoff, and this limitation becomes especially acute in defected structures where charged defects introduce slowly decaying electrostatic interactions.






However, there exist several important caveats with these findings. The synthetic benchmark, while instructive for isolating electrostatic behaviour, is by design an extreme test case: few real materials present interactions as purely long-range as formal point charges, and a model’s underperformance on this task should not be taken as disqualification for most applications. Similarly, the DFT benchmark metrics should not be interpreted as straightforward improvements over the synthetic case. The complexity of the DFT total energy, encompassing short-range repulsion, exchange-correlation, dispersion, and ionic self-energies, dilutes the electrostatic signal and could reduce the associated errors with electrostatics.






Looking forward, several extensions of this work can be considered. Phonon calculations and the evaluation of finite-temperature thermodynamic properties would test whether the long-range accuracy demonstrated in static benchmarks carries through to dynamical quantities. More complex defect structures, including higher vacancy concentrations and non-neutral supercells with explicit compensating charges, would probe the models’ robustness under conditions directly relevant to electrochemical applications such as solid-state batteries, where the repeated insertion and removal of ions leaves residual charge in the electrode material. Finally, a broader survey of strongly polar and ionic materials beyond SrTiO
3
 would establish the degree to which these conclusions generalise across the wider space of oxide and halide compounds where long-range electrostatics plays a central role.

title: LeanSide: A Formally Verified Co-Reasoning System for Natural-language Proofs
hypothesis:
We aim to build an informal-reasoning collaborative agent that makes
the power of formal verification accessible to broader audiences
who are trained to
reason in their own domains but have no knowledge of the formal language.
conclusion:
9. 
Discussion




In the previous section, we summarized students’ perceptions of the system: whether they could accurately assess system performance, when they were able to make progress, when they became stuck or diverted, and how their confidence changed. Here, we examine what explains these results. We distinguish findings that stem from current technical limitations from findings shaped by formally verified languages’ properties and our design choices. We then discuss design implications for future formally verified co-reasoning (FVCR) systems, including the limitation of formal languages, the design strategies that may address them, and the open challenges that remain. Table 
1
 summarizes five capabilities that a co-reasoning system may need and compares our system with the support provided by an LLM-based assistant and a formal debugger.






9.1. 
What results stem from technical limitations?




LeanSide was developed under the cost constraints of a classroom deployment, so each verification was optimized for responsiveness and resource use. Recent commercial auto-formalizers 
(
Achim et al., 2025
)
 report higher success rates in generating compiling proofs for correct Lean statements. Plugging stronger models into the pipeline would likely improve accuracy by reducing false negatives, and may also slightly reduce unfaithfulness. By contrast, we do not expect stronger provers to substantially change error-message understandability or most student behaviors around making progress or getting stuck, as these are more closely tied to the nature of formal verification and our system design choices.








9.2. 
What could an FVCR system provide?




We view an FVCR system like LeanSide could contributes four resources to a human-AI co-reasoning system: preserving the user’s reasoning path, providing low-false-positive validity checks, producing hallucination-free reasoning feedback, and helping users iteratively make implicit reasoning explicit.






First, our findings show that LeanSide can help 
preserve user agency through faithful representation
. Although we observed edge cases where the system unfaithfully auto-corrected step-level mistakes, LeanSide usually followed the user’s reasoning at the user’s granularity. This was not due to formal verification alone, but our system design choice for step-by-step auto-formalization. Prior work in human-AI collaboration has shown that LLM outputs can introduce useful directions, but can also unintentionally distract users from their original initiative 
(
Jakesch et al., 2023
; 
Levy et al., 2021
)
. Plausible but misaligned outputs can pull users away from their original line of reasoning, forcing them to monitor and repair the system or follow its suggested direction 
(
Subramonyam et al., 2024
; 
Mozannar et al., 2024
; 
Cros Vila and Sturm, 2025
)
. An FVCR system can reduce this risk by designing the system to always follow the user’s reasoning path. In our system, the unit of preservation is the pre-processed smallest progression unit: we do not require the system to preserve lower-level decompositions inside that unit. This unit is context-dependent and can be customized to the reasoning task. For example, in a tax-reasoning system, the unit might be one claimed inference: given a taxpayer’s income, deductions, filing status, or transaction history, the system would preserve the user’s intended application of a specific tax rule and then verify whether the stated tax consequence follows.






Second, our findings also shows an FVCR system can help 
localize errors through low-false-positive feedback
. Hallucination remains a persistent concern in high-stakes reasoning domains. LLM feedback can be unreliable in these settings because it may sound plausible while being logically wrong 
(
Kim et al., 2025
; 
Bo et al., 2025
; 
Spatharioti et al., 2025
)
. A formally verified backend can instead provide a stronger basis for accepting a step or conclusion when the translation is faithful. In our system, verified steps helped students narrow down the issue: once a step was verified, students gained confidence in its validity and could focus on unverified steps to correct faulty logic or fill the gaps. This process continued until all steps were verified, or until students used their mathematical knowledge to judge that a remaining unverified step reflected prover failure rather than their own error, as described in Section 
7.2
.






Third, an FVCR system can provide 
verified reasoning suggestions
. In our system, these traces appeared as continuation hints and as informal comments in the Lean code panel explaining how a step was proved. Both were natural-language explanations grounded in verified reasoning, and both were proven to be useful to students. Similar opportunities may arise in other reasoning tasks where users need more than a validity check mark: they also need natural-language explanations of why a step follows.






Finally, an FVCR system can help users make 
implicit reasoning explicit
. In our study, students often entered high-level or ambiguous reasoning, while the system returned less ambiguous informalizations at the user’s granularity. By comparing their input with these interpretations, students could notice ambiguity, clarify assumptions, and make their reasoning more rigorous. This suggests that formal verification can serve not only as a checker, but also as a mirror for helping users refine high-level strategies into precise reasoning.








9.3. 
LeanSide Limitations, and Design Implications for Future FVCR Systems




LeanSide was designed to isolate how formal language can support students’ proof iteration. Some of its limitations therefore come from deliberate design choices, which could help explain why students became stuck or diverged.






First, Lean error messages can reflect 
overly-granular reasoning
, which can confuse users. The limited understandability of step-level error messages illustrates this limitation. When students wrote a statement as a single assertion, they often treated it as not requiring further explanation in the course context. Lean errors, however, often reflected failures in lower-level proof obligations, making the feedback more granular than the student’s step and harder to interpret. This mismatch is difficult to solve through the Lean backbone alone. Complementary methods, such as sampling counterexamples or using an LLM to generate higher-level pedagogical and tutor-like feedback, can help produce more useful explanations (formal verification could also be used to check whether the LLM generated feedback before showing it to users).






The second limitation is that 
Lean may not follow the same strategic trace as human intuition
. In our study, students found the system useful for narrowing down local issues, but less able to guide them toward the right overall strategy. When a student followed an unproductive path, several mathematically correct steps could appear before the first incorrect step; the system flagged only the incorrect step, leaving the student to identify where the proof had diverged strategically. This reflects a mismatch between formal verification and human proof reasoning: Lean and search-based provers do not necessarily follow the intuitive order in which humans understand a proof, and may produce proofs that are counterintuitive or difficult to read 
(
Shi et al., 2025b
)
. Strategic hint generation, such as tree-search-based methods studied in existing tutoring systems, could therefore complement the formal verification backbone.






Together, what FVCR systems can provide and where they are limited offers guidance for future co-reasoning tool designers on when to use an FVCR system. It also suggests that, when using a formal verification system as the backbone, task-specific auxiliary components can add useful “meat” around formal verification, varying by domain and interaction need.






Figure 12. 
This figure compares two inspection scenarios: a general inspection scenario and inspection in an FVCR system. In the general scenario, users must inspect both interpretation and execution; in an FVCR system, the emphasis is primarily on inspecting interpretation.








9.4. 
Open design challenges: faithfulness checking and auto-detecting contextual granularity




One open design challenge is 
faithfulness checking
.
In figure 
12
, we summarize users’ inspection of a collaborative system into two categories (1) inspecting whether the system’s interpretation of the presented task is faithful, and (2) inspecting whether the system’s execution matches the user’s intent, which could be correspond to gulf of execution and evaluation 
(
Norman, 2013
)
. We view inspection in FVCR systems as a special case of this broader inspection problem, one that emphasizes (1) while placing less burden on (2).






In LeanSide, the side-by-side comparison between user input and system interpretation in the informalization panel makes faithfulness inspection explicit. The open design challenge is how to make these checks lightweight enough to avoid tedious interaction, while still keeping them visible enough to hold users’ attention.






We observed that students paid more attention to steps marked gray with error messages than to steps marked green, they did not always check whether the system had correctly interpreted what they meant in each sentence before everything is green.






To address this issue, our current design requires users to click “this is what I meant” or “not what I meant” for every informalized cell before submitting the assignment. If a user clicks “not what I meant,” the step returns to gray and the student must clarify and re-verify the proof. However, this design has limitations. Students usually checked every step only after resolving all error messages and preparing to submit the assignment. As a result, participants sometimes ignored unfaithful interpretations during intermediate iterations. However, an unfaithful earlier step could prevent later causally related steps from being verified, increasing the likelihood of inaccurate judgments and error messages for the later step. This is one reason participants became stuck or moved in the wrong direction, as discussed in Section 
8.3
.






We considered two alternative designs. First, after each verification, the system could require students to confirm “this is what I meant” or “not what I meant” before showing indicators and error messages. However, because informalizations often differ from the student’s original wording even when they are faithful, this interaction could become tedious. In addition, if a student clicked “not what I meant,” the system would need to regenerate the Lean interpretation, adding waiting time while leaving open the possibility that the new interpretation would still be unfaithful. Second, similar to existing LLM interfaces, the system could ask follow-up questions when the student’s input is ambiguous. We implemented this feature in the interface shown in Figure 
13
, but because it adds complexity beyond the scope of the present study, we leave its evaluation to future work.






Another open design challenge is 
auto-detecting contextual granularity
. Human users, such as students, often learn the acceptable granularity of reasoning from surrounding context, including lectures, peer discussion, and grading expectations, without anyone stating it explicitly. By contrast, LeanSide required substantial effort to construct a mini-lemma library that encoded this granularity, through rubric lemmas and side lemmas. Even with an automated pipeline, experts still had to inspect whether the specified granularity was appropriate. In mathematics education, this granularity is relatively visible because rubrics exist for each problem; in many other reasoning tasks, it may be far more implicit. A key open challenge for co-reasoning systems is therefore how they can learn the user’s expected granularity for communicating reasoning.






Figure 13. 
Follow up questions asked by the system when a student’s step is ambiguous










10. 
Limitations




This study has several limitations. First, the participant population was relatively homogeneous: all participants were recruited from the same university, and many were majoring in Computer Science, Mathematics, or related fields. This composition was partly a consequence of the course in which we deployed the system. Although none of the participants had prior experience with Lean, they may have been more familiar with formal verification than the general population and therefore more inclined to trust the verification results. In addition, their disciplinary training may have helped them express informal reasoning more precisely, making their inputs less ambiguous than those of general users.






Second, the problems selected for this study represent only a limited subset of mathematical reasoning, focusing primarily on Linear Algebra and Optimization. This choice was motivated by two factors: (1) the deployment course focused on Linear Algebra, and (2) the current auto-formalization and prover modules perform more reliably in these domains. Consequently, the observed results may not generalize to other areas of mathematics, where users may exhibit different input behaviors and where the system may face additional challenges.
