title: Growth by Intervention: State Demand and Preferential Allocation in the Hungarian Construction Sector since 2010
hypothesis:
Abstract 
This paper examines the post -2010 expansion of the Hungarian construction sector as a 
case study of large-scale government intervention in a single market.
conclusion:
9. Conclusion 
 
This paper examined the post -2010 expansion of Hungarian construction as a case study 
of large -scale government intervention, using a framework of two interconnected 
interventions to derive four testable propositions. The findings can be assessed proposition 
by proposition.  
Proposition 1 (overheating) is directly supported. Real construction output grew by around 
62% between 2010 and 2024, a rate matched in the region only by Romania and far above 
Poland, Czechia, Slovenia and Slovakia; but prices rose faster still. Construction producer 
prices outpaced the GDP deflator markedly from 2017 onward, peaking at a 10.5 
percentage point gap in 2022, and house prices rose faster than anywhere else in the EU. 
That a substantial part of the subsidies was absorbed into prices rather than reaching buyers 
is separately estimated for both principal instruments — roughly two-thirds of the CSOK 
grant and 60% of the VAT reduction (Banai et al., 2019; Fellner et al., 2019). 
Proposition 2 (rent -seeking signature) is supported as a pattern, though its interpretation 
remains inferential. Ownership of the leading firms shifted decisively from foreign to 
politically connected domestic hands; connected firms ’ return on equity ran two to three 
times that of other large firms throughout the period, while their exports remained 
negligible. Construction dominated public procurement, a domain in which low 
competition, preferential treatment of connected firms, and overpricing are independently 
documented (Fazekas et al., 2015; Tóth & Hajd u, 2018). What the data establish is the 
conjunction of high profitability, political connection, and weak exposure to competition; 
that this conjunction reflects rent extraction is an inference from the pattern, not a direct 
measurement of rent. 
Proposition 3 (productivity stagnation) is directly supported. Labour productivity per hour 
worked made no net progress, returning by 2024 to roughly its 2000 level. The comparison 
with Romania is instructive: the region’s other outlier in output and investment growth saw 
construction productivity rise by roughly half over the same period. Nor did the investment 
surge translate into productive capacity in the expected way — while sector-wide gross 
fixed capital formation r ose by 278%, connected firms ’ growth was increasingly 
acquisitive, the tangible share of their assets falling from 55% to 26% as the balance shifted 
into financial holdings and equity stakes rather than new capacity. 
Proposition 4 (uneven distribution) is supported in aggregate. Connected firms captured a 
rising share of sector profits, from around 16% to 56%; households received subsidies 
whose value was partly eroded by the price increases those subsidies induced; an d the 
sector as a whole grew larger and more profitable without becoming more productive. 
What the evidence does not yet establish is the household-level incidence — which groups 
of buyers ultimately bore the capitalised subsidy. 
The central interpretive claim — that these patterns jointly reflect subsidy capitalisation 
and politically mediated rent extraction — is a disciplined inference. The capitalisation 
mechanism rests on direct price and volume evidence and on well-identified findings from 
comparable settings (Fellner et al., 2019; Kunovac & Zilic, 2022; Carozzi et al., 2024). The 
rent-extraction mechanism rests on the conjunction of procurement, ownership, and 
profitability patterns that matches the international signature of politically connected firms 
(Fisman, 2001; Faccio, 2006) and the independent estimate t hat construction profits grew 
disproportionately among Hungarian large firms (Bartha, 2026). The competing 
explanations considered in Section 3.7 — post-crisis catch-up, global cost shocks, labour 
shortages, and the EU funds cycle — each could account for part of the picture, and several 
amplified the dynamics described here. None of them, however, explains why recovery 
took this exceptional form only in Hungary, why prices diverged before the global 
inflationary episode, or why the gains concentrated in politically connected firms. 
The analysis has clear limitations. It is descriptive: it establishes consistency with the 
framework rather than identifying causal effects, and it cannot quantify how much of the 
price divergence is attributable to each policy instrument, nor how much of the profitability 
surge constitutes rent rather than return. The firm -level evidence covers only the largest 
companies, and its composition changes over time. Political connection is identified from 
ownership records and the published classifications of connected individuals; while this 
yields a documented and reproducible list, it captures only connections visible in ownership 
data and so represents a lower bound. 
These limitations define the open questions. A counterfactual exercise — what housing 
output the subsidy outlays would have purchased under elastic supply — could quantify 
the welfare cost of capitalisation. Measuring the household -level incidence of the e roded 
subsidies — which groups of buyers ultimately bore the capitalised cost — would require 
linked transaction and subsidy data, and deserves a study of its own. 
The analysis carries direct implications for policy design. First, demand -side housing and 
infrastructure programmes should be conditioned on the supply capacity of the targeted 
sector: where supply is inelastic, subsidies are predictably capitalised into prices, and the 
larger the stimulus, the greater the share absorbed by sellers rather than the intended 
beneficiaries. Stimulus paired with supply -side measures — workforce development, 
predictable long-term programming, stable regulatory horizons — is less likely to dissipate 
into prices. Second, the temporal design of interventions matters as much as their size: 
temporary and cyclical instruments, such as time-limited VAT preferences and electorally 
timed investment surges, discourage the capacity investment that would make the stimulus 
effective, so credible multi-year commitments should be preferred to renewable short-term 
schemes. Third, the effectiveness of any demand expansion depends on the integrity of its 
allocation: where procurement competition is weak, additional public spending raises the 
rents available to connected firms rather than output, implying that competitive tendering 
safeguards and transparency requirements are not merely governa nce concerns but 
preconditions for the stimulus to reach its target. Finally, for EU policy specifically, the 
findings suggest that the volume of cohesion funding matters less than the procurement 
institutions through which it flows — strengthening conditi onality on competitive 
allocation may do more for real outcomes than adjusting funding levels. 
The broader lesson extends beyond Hungary. Demand -side stimulus and politically 
structured procurement are common policy instruments; what the Hungarian construction 
sector illustrates is their interaction. Demand expansion under inelastic supply inflates 
prices; preferential allocation converts inflated prices into concentrated rents; and rents, 
once available, weaken the competitive pressure that drives productivity — leaving a sector 
that is larger, more profitable, and no more efficient than before. Where these instruments 
are combined, extensive growth without efficiency is not an anomaly but a predictable

6. Discussion 
6.1. Mobility advantages are organizationally situated 
Research on scientific mobility has established that internationally mobile scientists often publish more, 
receive greater recognition, and maintain more international collaborations (Cruz-Castro & Sanz-Menéndez, 
2010; Jonkers & Cruz-Castro, 2013). More recent work has provided more contextualized interpretations by 
showing that mobility outcomes depend on career trajectories, organizational contexts, and the networks 
through which scientists access knowledge (Benz & Larivière, 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Capponi and Frenken 
(2025) similarly demonstrate that the consequences of academic training depend on the institutional and 
intellectual context in which training occurs. Our findings extend this contextual turn from mobility 
trajectories to destination-system structure. Foreign-trained faculty contribute disproportionately to highly 

 
20 
cited U.S. research, but citation differences narrow sharply when faculty are compared within the same 
institution, domain, rank, and year. At the same time, differences in publication volume and mixed-training-
origin collaboration remain. Thus, the foreign-training advantage contains two analytically distinct 
components: differential placement within the research system and differences that persist within comparable 
organizational settings. 
This distinction modifies how mobility premiums should be interpreted. Organizational position is not merely 
a confounder separating foreign training from its “net” effect. Internationally trained researchers enter a highly 
stratified destination system, and their observed contribution partly reflects where that system places them. The 
meaningful objective is therefore not to detach mobility from context, but to situate it with comparable 
scientific capabilities to organizational environments. Accordingly, our study connects mobility research with 
organizational cumulative advantage and academic hierarchy (Clauset et al., 2015; Wapman et al., 2022; Way 
et al., 2019). 
6.2. International mobility carries relational capital, not simply additional ties 
The collaboration network results expand the literature on the benefit of having elevated scientific networks. 
Existing literature found migrant and return scientists possess larger international networks and international 
connections can constitute scientific social capital by providing access to foreign knowledge and collaborators 
(Franzoni et al., 2014; Scellato et al., 2015).  Our results add a different dimension: foreign-trained faculty not 
only have greater prior collaborator reach and breadth, they also received higher return on elite output because 
of their wider collaboration compared with U.S.-trained faculty. This pattern is stable across alternative 
network windows and broadly similar across scientific domains. The result extends the literature from network 
possession to the relationship between network position and subsequent scientific performance. 
That distinction matters for social capital. Our evidence suggests that the relationship between connectivity and 
scientific output depends partly on the trajectory through which that connectivity was accumulated. One 
possibility, consistent with Scellato et al. (2015), is that networks spanning training systems contain 
complementary or less redundant resources. The heterogeneity across terminal-degree countries reinforces this 
point. Our country results showed substantial variation in the network–output relationship across training 
systems. Such systems may differ in their connectivity to U.S. science, institutional pathways, and migration 
selectivity. International training should therefore be understood as a heterogeneous source of relational 
capital.  
6.3. Mobility and knowledge recombination 
A third explanation links mobility to knowledge recombination. International mobility exposes scientists to 
new research environments, collaborators, and ideas, potentially enabling exploration beyond established 
knowledge bases. A recent study has shown that mobility increased research quality alongside collaboration 
with new, higher-quality coauthors and exploration of new topics (Baruffaldi et al., 2020), which complements 
broader research linking novel knowledge combinations to scientific impact (Uzzi et al., 2013).  
Our results place an important boundary on this explanation. Foreign-trained faculty appear cognitively 
broader in raw comparisons, but this difference disappears once the larger size of their prior publication 
portfolios is considered. Their distinctive collaboration reach therefore does not translate into correspondingly 
broader individual topic portfolios. 
This separation of social reach from cognitive breadth suggests that access to heterogeneous knowledge may 
instead be organized through collaborators. In this sense, our findings complement the recombination 
argument, which suggests that one consequence of international training may reside in the social distribution of 
knowledge across relationships, rather than in greater cognitive diversification within individual portfolios 
(Wang, 2016). 
 
21 
6.4. International training as a feature of scientific capacity 
These results connect literatures that have largely examined different parts of the same process. Mobility 
research has established that scientists carry knowledge and relationships across borders (Cruz-Castro & Sanz-
Menéndez, 2010; Edler et al., 2011; Franzoni et al., 2014; Jonkers & Cruz-Castro, 2013; Scellato et al., 2015). 
Research on scientific careers shows that the consequences of mobility and training depend on trajectories and 
contexts (Baruffaldi & Landoni, 2012; Baruffaldi et al., 2020; Benz & Larivière, 2025). Network research, 
meanwhile, shows that access to international connections can affect scientific performance (Chen et al., 
2025). Our study brings these arguments together at the level of the destination research system. Its principal 
contribution is to show that international training is associated with three separable features of scientific 
capacity: organizational structure, collaboration networks, and research portfolio.  
6.5. Limitations and future research 
Foreign-trained faculty employed at U.S. universities are selected through training, migration, hiring, and 
career progression, while network position is itself shaped by prior productivity, reputation, resources, and 
scientific specialization. The analyses identify organizational and relational patterns, not selection mechanisms 
of foreign-trained faculty into U.S. universities or causal effects of foreign training or collaborator reach. 
Terminal-degree location captures only one element of mobility history. Studies showed the importance of 
using complete career trajectories in measuring mobility effect (Benz & Larivière, 2025) and the stage at 
which international movement occurs is related to subsequent network structure (Scellato et al., 2015). Future 
research should therefore reconstruct sequences of doctoral training, postdoctoral mobility, institutional 
movement, and international collaboration. Last, coauthorship captures only publication ties and does not 
reveal other relationships such as mentorship or tacit knowledge transfer. These constraints provide boundaries 
of the interpretations of the obtained results.

Conclusion




This paper is a diagnostic study of LLM robustness to numerical claim perturbations. Standard fine-tuning teaches the model to confirm a claim’s surface form rather than verify it against evidence, and accuracy on label-flipping inputs collapses to single digits. Adversarial fine-tuning on counterfactual examples recovers near-perfect accuracy, with small QLoRA-tuned models (0.6B–8B) surpassing zero-shot 32B and frontier closed-source baselines on the hardest perturbations. Composition matters more than variety: 
Masked
 and 
Numeration
 are essential, 
Approximation
 and 
Random
 redundant. Robustness also transfers across languages and domains without target-language data, suggesting a generalised numerical decision boundary rather than memorised edits.










Limitations




Data and perturbation scope.




Our perturbation taxonomy rewrites numerical expressions in the claim while leaving evidence unchanged. Section 
5.7
 reaches the evidence side through VitaminC’s human-authored revisions, but our generator does not produce them, and jointly perturbing claim and evidence remains an open direction. The six types focus on scalar quantities as digits or written-out numbers, so robustness to unit conversions, date arithmetic, compound quantities, or numbers in tables is not guaranteed. Training and primary evaluation use QuanTemp (English fact-checking); cross-dataset experiments add Spanish, AVeriTeC and VitaminC but remain in English and Spanish and, apart from VitaminC’s single-sentence evidence, within the fact-checking domain, so broader language coverage and generalisation to scientific, financial, or tabular settings both require further evaluation.








Model and evaluation setup.




Experiments use only the Qwen3 family (0.6B–32B) with QLoRA and soft prompt tuning. 
Aarnes and Setty (2025)
 document the same numerical brittleness on LLaMA-family models, so we expect the qualitative findings to hold across LLaMA, Mistral, Gemma, and comparable open families, though confirming this directly is left for future work; quantitative effects (the scale at which diminishing returns set in, the size of the QLoRA-vs.-soft-prompt gap) may shift across families and PEFT methods. The soft-prompt baseline reuses QLoRA hyperparameters, making it a matched-budget rather than optimally tuned comparison. All experiments assume gold evidence, isolating verification from retrieval; whether the robustness gains survive noisy or incomplete retrieval is left for future work.








Interpretability.




We lack a mechanistic account of 
why
 adversarial fine-tuning works. It is unclear whether models learn to attend more carefully to numerical tokens, develop surface-form-invariant representations, or rely on other signals; attribution, probing, and activation-patching analyses would be needed to explain the gains and anticipate failure modes — a direction we intend to pursue.










Ethical Considerations




This work studies the robustness of LLMs used for numerical claim verification. We identify specific weaknesses that existing models exhibit when claims contain perturbed numerical expressions, and we show that adversarial fine-tuning substantially reduces these vulnerabilities. We do not endorse any specific model or configuration for deployment in real-world fact-checking pipelines; fact-checking is a nuanced task where model outputs should be treated as decision-support tools rather than authoritative verdicts, and human oversight remains essential.






The perturbation techniques studied could, in principle, be used to craft adversarial claims that evade automated fact-checkers. We consider this a reason to publish rather than withhold the findings: understanding and documenting these failure modes is a prerequisite for building more resilient systems, and the perturbation types we study are straightforward enough that they are already available to any motivated adversary. All data used in this work is sourced from publicly available fact-checking corpora, and no personal or sensitive information is involved.

Conclusions and Future Work




We introduced a simple logical framework for norm-guided decision making under uncertainty.
Starting from a restricted fragment of Chellas’ Minimal Deontic Logic, we identified a language
where deontic reasoning reduces to classical propositional reasoning while retaining obligations
and prohibitions over atomic actions. We extended this fragment with explicitly represented
conditional norms and factual detachment, obtaining a lightweight deontic logic.






To reason under incomplete information, we combined the framework with multi-agent doxastic logic,
allowing norms to depend on agents’ beliefs and beliefs about norms. We introduced the Doxastic
Norm Compliance Optimization Problem (DNCOP), where an agent selects decisions minimizing weighted
norm violations. By distinguishing optimization relative to the agent’s beliefs from optimization
relative to the objective state of the world, the framework captures a key aspect of autonomous
decision making under uncertainty. We identified locality and truthfulness conditions under which
these perspectives coincide, guaranteeing that subjectively optimal decisions are also objectively
optimal.






The framework also admits efficient computation. For local, decision-sound DNCOPs, we showed that
optimal decisions can be found by a polynomial-time reduction to weighted partial MaxSAT,
leveraging mature optimization techniques while preserving logical rigour and transparency.






The framework deliberately favors simplicity over expressiveness. Restricting normative contents to
atomic propositions enables reductions to propositional reasoning and straightforward integration
with epistemic formalisms, while still covering a broad range of practical decision-making
scenarios. Its modular design leaves room for richer normative and epistemic extensions.

title: Comparison of Common Crawl News & GDELT
hypothesis: This paper directly compares GDELT and CC-News, two publicly available and widely used news datasets. Analyzing each dataset, we seek to compare GDELT and CC-News while highlighting their strengths and limitations.
conclusion:
Conclusion and Future Work




In an era where data plays a pivotal role in shaping decisions, solving problems, and advancing systems, the storage and accessibility of information are paramount. Web archiving fosters innovation and academic research in our digital age. However, many web archives are limited due to restricted public access or technological and copyright constraints. The GDELT project and Common Crawl have emerged as pioneers, offering extensive, freely available big data that contributes significantly to the academic community.






This paper presents a comparative analysis of two prominent news datasets: GDELT and CC-News. Our research examines various aspects of each dataset, including size, diversity, news source quality, and language distribution. Through this exploration, we provided beneficial insights to the computational journalism and social science communities. Researchers should weigh the distinct characteristics of these datasets when selecting datasets for their studies.






To conclude, GDELT, with its collection spanning traditional news sources worldwide, presents a comprehensive and diverse range of information within its news data. On the other hand, CC-News, derived from the Common Crawl, offers a higher volume of news data and provides a perspective on other web-based news content. We found the largest differences between the two datasets in their news sources. Furthermore, our comparative analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of each dataset, allowing researchers to make informed choices based on their specific study requirements, not limited to utilizing both datasets simultaneously to leverage the unique characteristics of each fully.






In future work, we will classify news articles by topic to better analyze the composition of the content of each dataset. Conclusion




This study establishes the first benchmark for the joint hetero-modal segmentation of co-occurring white matter hyperintensities (WMH) and ischaemic stroke lesions (ISL). By leveraging a unique, fully annotated, multi-sequence dataset, we demonstrated that hetero-modal learning effectively overcomes the rigid data requirements of traditional modality specialist models. Rather than discarding incomplete scans, this approach maximises the utility of all available data. We showed this to be effective in data-constrained scenarios, with hetero-modal models generally outperforming modality specialist baselines.






Beyond accommodating missing data during training, our findings highlight the adaptability of hetero-modal networks at inference. When trained on disjointed datasets sharing only a single anchor modality, these models successfully generalised to novel modality combinations, maintaining robust predictive performance even when the highly informative FLAIR sequence was unavailable.






Additionally, we address a major hurdle in clinical deployment: silent data degradation. By introducing the Multimodal Attention Router (MMAR) block alongside a complimentary corruption augmentation strategy, we showed that this proof-of-concept method can dynamically adapt to unflagged, catastrophically corrupted modalities. Through spatially adaptive feature routing, the MMAR-based model learns to treat severely degraded regions in scans as missing, preserving segmentation accuracy in the presence of extreme noise, bias fields, and false-present modalities.






Ultimately, these strategies offer a robust and practical pathway for developing and deploying medical image segmentation tools in imperfect, real-world clinical environments.






Limitations




We acknowledge several limitations in this study.
First, it is likely that our comparative results are highly sensitive to the total volume and modality distribution of the training data; we urge caution when extrapolating our results to other data distributions.
Second, due to the number of individual training runs required and limited computational resources, our evaluations are centred on a single random training, validation, and test split, and each model was trained only once. While we attempted to mitigate the impact of these factors by performing statistical significance tests, we must highlight this limitation.
Third, our evaluation relies solely on the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC). Although DSC has known limitations, it remains the standard segmentation metric and correlates strongly with other measures. Since our primary objective was the relative comparison of methods rather than establishing absolute task performance, limiting our evaluation to DSC allowed us to reduce the complexity of the results while preserving statistical power.
Fourth, due to a lack of truly corrupted scans in our dataset, test time corruption transformations were required for evaluating the models that were trained for corruption-robustness, using corruption augmentation. To mitigate this bias, we applied different transformation parameters during training and testing augmentations.
Finally, because our primary motivation was to evaluate the viability of hetero-modal learning in data-starved clinical scenarios, we opted for foundational, proven baseline methods. Conclusion




This paper investigated the interaction between DP-SGD, ghost clipping, and weight tying in decoder-only language models. Through theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on GPT2 and DistilGPT2, we showed that the benefits of weight tying observed in standard non-private training do not naturally transfer to the differentially private setting. Across both models, untied embeddings consistently achieved superior privacy–utility–efficiency trade-offs, improving predictive performance and optimization stability while preserving the substantial memory savings provided by ghost clipping.






A key contribution is identifying a limitation of ghost clipping under tied embeddings. Consequently, treating the two pathway contributions as independent parameter blocks omits their cross-term and does not recover the exact norm of the shared parameter.
Although exact norms can be restored by including the missing cross-term, this requires materializing gradient interactions, which ghost clipping aims to avoid.






Taken together, these findings demonstrate that scalable differentially private optimization is not fully architecture-agnostic. Its correctness depends on how architectural choices shape gradient structure. Ghost clipping remains exact and effective when parameters are disjoint, but tied embeddings violate its assumptions. This highlights the need to jointly design model architectures and privacy-preserving optimization methods for efficient private foundation models.

Motivated by practical issues with implementation of IPEA, a popular iterative algorithm well suited for for phase estimation on NISQ and early FT hardware, we consider the problem of allocation of number of shots across iterations. Different iterations of IPEA consume different amounts of resource in terms of circuit complexity, oracle call, etc., depending on the particular phase estimation problem, e.g., phase estimation for order finding versus that for different quantum simulations. We find the optimal allocation of number of shots (repetitions) per iteration that maximizes the probability of success of the overall IPEA algorithm, given a budget for the total resource. We derive closed-form expressions for optimal number of shots for different scalings of cost and reliability with iterations. We do so by obtaining upper and lower surrogates for the objective by invoking tight concentration and anti-concentration bounds ad showing that their solutions are the same for low noise. In this regime, we obtain a simple thumb rule for resource allocation that does not need to know exact scalings of the individual costs or total resource. The starting premise of this work was to show how measurements on dynamical quantum systems can reveal not only the fluctuations of the quantity measured but also other system observables and properties.






A previously studied model with a particle moving on a lattice with a single weakly probed site

Our results show that the interplay between energetic constraints, spatial connectivity, and individual competition strongly shapes territorial organization in systems of competing males. Using an individual-based spatial model, we show how these factors jointly regulate the persistence of males, the distribution of territory sizes, and the emergence of unequal territorial structures (see a schematic representation of our results in Fig. 
10
). Although the model considers a single species and only intraspecific competition, the results reveal mechanisms that resemble patterns predicted by broader ecological theories of competition and coexistence.






In classical Lotka-Volterra competition models and in Modern Coexistence Theory, coexistence among competitors is expected when intraspecific competition is stronger than interspecific competition. However, these approaches are typically phenomenological and summarize competitive interactions through simple terms such as

These costs limit territorial expansion and prevent the progressive exclusion of competitors, ultimately stabilizing both the number of males and the distribution of territories. Moreover, the model allows us to explore how these competitive costs interact with other ecological factors, such as resource distribution and spatial connectivity.






Landscape connectivity emerges in our simulations as a key factor shaping the outcome of territorial competition. Connectivity, understood here as the structural continuity between resource patches, has long been recognized as an important determinant of ecosystem functioning and species persistence 
[
41
, 
18
]
. In our model, connectivity is controlled by the seeds propagation parameter 
α
\alpha
, which determines how resources spread across the matrix. Different levels of connectivity generate markedly different territorial outcomes: highly connected matrices promote strong competition and the exclusion of many males, whereas fragmented resource distributions allow more individuals to maintain territories. This shows that simple changes in spatial structure can produce non-linear effects on population organization.






From this perspective, matrix connectivity may play a role similar to that proposed by disturbance-based coexistence mechanisms. Reduced connectivity can create spatial refuges that limit direct interactions between dominant and subordinate individuals, allowing smaller or less competitive males to maintain territories. In this sense, spatial fragmentation can operate analogously to the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis at the intraspecific level, preventing the monopolization of resources by a few dominant individuals 
[
17
, 
61
]
. However, this mechanism must be interpreted in conjunction with energetic constraints, since body size strongly affects locomotion costs according to the allometric relationship described by Taylor and Heglund 
[
66
]
.






The model also reveals interesting parallels with systems studied in econophysics. In simulations without confrontation costs, the number of males declines continuously while the distribution of territorial areas converges toward a stable configuration. Similar dynamics have been observed in economic exchange models, where interactions among agents lead to stable but highly unequal wealth distributions 
[
55
, 
19
, 
29
]
. Such analogies contribute to a growing body of research exploring conceptual links between ecological and economic systems, particularly in terms of resource allocation and competition among agents 
[
62
, 
7
, 
68
]
.






Territorial organization also has important implications for population structure and reproductive dynamics. In wild camelids, territorial males defend resource-rich areas in order to attract and retain females. Consequently, variation in territory size may translate into differences in reproductive success, survival, and ultimately genetic contribution to future generations 
[
26
, 
76
, 
3
, 
56
]
. Our results suggest that highly connected and energetically rich environments tend to concentrate resources into fewer territories, potentially reducing genetic diversity by increasing reproductive inequality among males. Conversely, stronger confrontation costs tend to favor the persistence of more males with positive balances, and therefore stable territories, and a more distributed reproductive structure.






These findings complement previous theoretical work on the social organization of wild camelids. In a previous study we had analyzed how female distribution emerges from the interaction between territory quality, male performance, and the presence of bachelor males in the system 
[
31
]
. Combining both approaches suggests that highly productive and well-connected environments may generate social contexts where many males fail to secure territories and instead adopt harassment strategies. Under these conditions, females may prefer to form larger groups despite the potential costs associated with resource competition within groups. Such dynamics can further increase inequality in the distribution of females among territories, adding another layer of complexity to the system.






Our modeling approach is also related to economic models of animal territoriality, which interpret territorial behavior as the outcome of cost–benefit optimization strategies. Many of these models assume that individuals adjust their behavior to maximize energetic benefits relative to costs affecting fitness 
[
53
, 
21
, 
3
, 
35
, 
36
]
. However, most of these models are deterministic, non-spatial, and focus on the decision-making process of a single territorial resident. In contrast, our model explicitly incorporates spatial structure and the simultaneous interaction of multiple competing males, allowing the emergent territorial configuration to arise from decentralized individual decisions.






Another important component of our model is the explicit incorporation of allometric constraints. Locomotion costs associated with territorial patrol depend strongly on body mass and biomechanical limitations. These energetic costs ultimately influence the size and stability of territories, linking individual physiological traits with population-level spatial organization 
[
63
, 
11
, 
15
, 
9
]
. In this sense, the energetic balance framework provides a mechanistic bridge between individual traits and emergent social structures.






Finally, it is important to compare our model outcomes with empirical observations. In wild camelids, typical territory sizes range between approximately 13 and 46 hectares 
[
42
, 
76
, 
5
, 
64
]
. Some of our simulations, particularly those with very high connectivity, generate territories larger than these values. In real systems, several ecological factors (that are not included in the model) may constrain territorial expansion, including selective grazing, habitat visibility, predation risk, and interactions with other members of the family group. Nevertheless, large territories have been reported in some guanaco populations, reaching between 200 and 900 hectares in certain contexts 
[
48
]
.






Regarding energetic inputs, the main grasses consumed by wild camelids belong to genera such as 
Stipa
, 
Poa
 and 
Panicum

[
8
, 
58
, 
57
, 
40
, 
32
, 
65
, 
50
, 
49
, 
31
]

In summary, our study illustrates how territorial organization can emerge from the interaction between energetic constraints, spatial structure and individual competition. By explicitly linking allometric scaling to competitive dynamics, the framework provides a mechanistic perspective connecting individual physiology to population-level patterns. Beyond camelids, these results suggest that incorporating energetic and spatial constraints into models of territoriality may be essential for understanding the diversity and stability of social systems in vertebrates.

We have proposed a classification of fault tolerant quantum phases based on the ability to robustly transfer encoded information between convex sets of states using shallow quantum-local circuits. Our work makes explicit the connection between quantum fault tolerance and quantum phases of matter which are robust to noise. While it has been known that topological orders can encode logical information and serve as quantum memories, we extend the notion of preserving information encoded within a phase to a set of active operations which can be implemented on quantum devices, notably including circuits with measurements and feedback.






In our classification, stability, i.e., the existence of a nonzero recovery threshold for local noise, is a property of an entire phase. title: LLM-as-a-Judge for Low-Resource Languages: Adapting Ragas and Comparative Ranking for Romanian
hypothesis:
Abstract


Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems remains a challenge for Low-Resource Languages (LRLs), where standard reference-based metrics fall short. This paper investigates the viability of the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm for Romanian by adapting the Ragas framework using next-generation models (Gemini 2.5 and Gemini 3). By leveraging these newer, more powerful models, we aim to establish a robust baseline for automated RAG evaluation in Romanian, providing a transferable strategy for other low-resource languages.
conclusion:
8 
Conclusion and Future Work




This study bridges a gap in the evaluation of RAG systems for Low-Resource Languages. By introducing 
AdminRo-Eval
 and benchmarking three automated evaluation strategies, we demonstrated that English-centric metrics cannot be blindly transferred to Romanian without performance degradation.






Our experiments reveal that the "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is viable for Romanian, provided the methodology is tailored to the specific metric. We found that the granular decomposition of the Ragas framework is superior for objective metrics like 
Faithfulness
 (96% alignment with Gemini 2.5 Pro), whereas Comparative Ranking is more effective for nuanced semantic judgments like 
Answer Relevance
 (90% alignment). Furthermore, our results caution against the use of lightweight "Flash" models for complex reasoning tasks in LRLs, as evidenced by their inability to accurately assess Context Relevance. Ultimately, while newer models like Gemini 3 Pro excel in specific areas, the older Gemini 2.5 Pro architecture provided the most robust and consistent baseline for Romanian RAG evaluation.






To further advance RAG evaluation for under-represented languages, we propose to expand the AdminRo-Eval dataset beyond public administration to include medical and legal domains, where hallucination risks carry higher stakes. Also, reliance on proprietary models (Gemini/GPT) limits accessibility for the LRL community, so we would want to assess the efficacy of open-weights models (e.g., Llama 3, Mistral) as judges also.








9 
Limitations




Our study faces three primary limitations. First, the 
AdminRo-Eval
 dataset focuses exclusively on formal public administration documents. Findings may not generalize to open-domain or informal contexts where semantic ambiguity is higher. Second, the modest size of our manually annotated ground truth (100 samples) limits the statistical power. Third, since Gemini was used to generate the synthetic test data, the high agreement scores may partially reflect a ’self-enhancement’ bias, where the model preferentially favors its own generation style.








10 
Ethics Statement




This work utilizes the 
AdminRo-Eval
 dataset, which was constructed exclusively from public documents available on official Romanian government websites. We performed manual verification to ensure that no sensitive Personally Identifiable Information (PII) of private citizens was included in the corpus. Regarding the human evaluation, the native speaker annotators were volunteers. While our research aims to enhance the factual reliability of RAG systems, we acknowledge that the "Judge" models (Gemini) may still exhibit biases inherent in their pre-training data. We emphasize that automated evaluation tools for the public sector are intended to assist human decision-making, not to replace human oversight in administrative processes.

In this paper, we aimed to investigate inﬂation and isotropization in th e early Universe within
the phantom model. The phantom model is one of the successful mo dels for describing the late-
time acceleration of the Universe. In principle, from the perspectiv e of unifying gravitational mod-
els, cosmological models should provide an adequate description of a ll stages of cosmic evolution,
including the earliest moments of its origin and phenomena such as inﬂa tion and isotropization.
This was one of the motivations for the present investigation.
We examined three backgrounds—BI, BIII, and KS—with ﬁve diﬀere nt well-known forms of
the potential in the phantom model, corresponding to ﬁfteen diﬀer ent cases.
To this end, we ﬁrst extended the well-known cosmic no-hair theore m (Heusler theorem) to
phantom model containing any form of convex potentials. We found that, irrespective of the
36
restrictions that this theorem imposes on the constant paramete rs of the potential and on the
behaviour of the phantom ﬁeld, it ultimately cannot provide an adequ ate answer because the
shear scalar and the expansion rate vanish simultaneously. We ther efore continued the analysis
using the dynamical-systems approach.
We have sought to keep the analysis as general as possible. In tota l, we identiﬁed 87 critical
points and analysed their stability and cosmological properties. Mos t of the critical points were
non-hyperbolic, and we consequently analysed their centre manifo lds. Our approach to the centre-
manifold analysis was based on the perturbation method, with a prec ision of 10 −4 . More than
550 ﬁgures were generated during the stability analysis using this me thod.
In the dynamical-systems analysis, we ﬁrst speciﬁed that, for the ﬁfteen combinations (models)
under consideration, we sought to achieve one of the following two o bjectives:
1. a saddle critical point that simultaneously describes inﬂationary e xpansion and strong
isotropization;
2. two saddle critical points in a ﬁxed background and potential, one describing inﬂationary
expansion and the other strong isotropization on an expanding man ifold.
It should be noted that, unlike studies that allow attractor points, we regarded only saddle
points as physical. Our reasoning is that the Universe passes throu gh these points, and points
along its evolutionary trajectory are of saddle type, apart from t he initial and ﬁnal points of the
Universe, which may be repeller and attractor, respectively.
For convenience and to summarize the main results, we considered ﬁ ve important classes:
• Class I: Inﬂation alone, without either weak or strong isotr opization.
In this case, only the BIII Universe produced physically acceptable points, for all potentials
except potential D.
• Class II: Weak isotropization alone in an expanding Univers e, without inﬂation.
With the exception of the BIII Universe, both of the remaining back grounds, i.e. BI and KS,
produced acceptable critical points for all the potentials. In this c ase, the two backgrounds
exhibited essentially similar behaviour: in both, the phantom ﬁeld and t he corresponding
potential were inactive at the critical points and were instead froz en. The constant pa-
rameters of the potential functions did not appear in the eigenvalu es either, and therefore
could not be used to adjust the stability, although the saddle points themselves existed and
required no such adjustment.
• Class III: Strong isotropization alone in an expanding Univ erse, without inﬂa-
tion.
None of the backgrounds produced this behaviour for any of the p otentials considered. This
cancel the existence of the second option mentioned above.
• Class IV: Inﬂationary expansion accompanied by weak isotro pization.
With the exception of the BIII Universe, both of the remaining back grounds, i.e. BI and
KS, produced physically acceptable critical points for potentials B, C, and D. This was the
best and most physically desirable outcome that we obtained. In oth er words, it was the
optimal outcome among the ﬁfteen cases considered.
Unlike in Class II, the fact that both the BI and KS backgrounds pro duced critical points
satisfying the conditions of this class does not imply that these back grounds have approx-
imately equivalent eﬀects and roles. In both backgrounds, the con stant parameters of the
37
potential functions appeared in the eigenvalues and helped make it p ossible to adjust the
stability of the points to saddle type. In this sense, they played a ro le. However, a pro-
nounced and signiﬁcant diﬀerence between the two backgrounds in producing points in this
class was that, in the BI Universe, the contributions of the potent ial and the phantom ﬁeld
to the kinetic contribution were zero, and the phantom ﬁeld was eﬀe ctively inactive. In the
KS Universe, by contrast, both the potentials and the phantom ﬁe ld were active and had
non-negligible time dependence.
Combining the ﬁndings of this class with those of Class II, and eliminatin g by symmetry
the role of the constant parameters in the potential functions in t he eigenvalues of both the
BI and KS backgrounds, one may infer that the role of the potentia l and the scalar ﬁeld
of the phantom model in producing desirable critical points vanishes and is frozen in the
BI Universe. In the KS Universe, however, they may or may not play a role, depending on
what is required.
• Class V: Inﬂationary expansion accompanied by strong isotr opization.
No physically acceptable critical point was found for any case in the p hantom model.
A summary of our ﬁndings, without referring to the names of the po ints and focusing only
on the ability of each potential to produce the corresponding critic al points in the diﬀerent
backgrounds studied in the phantom cosmological model, is present ed in Table 2 11.

combinations leading to 87 critical points, we found neither a saddle c ritical point that simulta-
neously describes inﬂationary expansion and strong isotropization , nor at least two saddle critical

weak or strong, and then only for all potentials except poten tial D. Therefore, it appears that,
unlike the BIII Universe, the BI and KS Universes are more rea sonable choices for describing the

were therefore unable to change the nature of the critical points using the parameter associated

very helpful in analysing the critical points. For the other potentia ls, by contrast, the constant
parameters of the potentials played the primary role in determining t he stability of most critical
points. This may have contributed to their greater success, altho ugh the existence of potential E
changes this proposition from a suﬃcient condition to a necessary o ne. An interesting feature of
potential E was that most of its points corresponded to a canonica l ﬁeld rather than a phantom
ﬁeld12; that is, it automatically produced points associated with canonical, rather than phantom,
ﬁelds. For this reason, and in view of the discussion in Subsection 4.3, it may be argued that
potential E is more suitable for a canonical ﬁeld than for a phantom ﬁ eld.
We argued that failure to achieve the main objective of the paper—t he occurrence of inﬂation
and strong isotropization in the phantom model for a ﬁxed backgro und and potential—does not
imply a deﬁciency in the phantom model. We discussed this issue in detail in Section 4.4. If
all potentials and backgrounds considered in the literature were te sted during inﬂation and post-
inﬂation stages, and strong isotropization were not conﬁrmed, on e could then suspect a deﬁciency

universally for the phantom model with diﬀerent potentials: they ar e sometimes correct and
sometimes not. This makes it necessary to avoid theorems that issu e general conclusions in these

canonical ﬁeld and argued that, unlike the phantom ﬁeld, the canon ical ﬁeld can achieve our

with hyperbolic-type potentials in describing the early Un iverse, although the phantom model per-

In this work, the structural, energetic, magnetic, electronic, mechanical, dynamical, and thermal 
properties of a  novel two-dimensional CeN monolayer derived from the (111) orientation of the 
bulk rocksalt CeN  structure were systematically investigated using first -principles calculations. 
The reduction from the three -dimensional bulk structure to the two -dimensional limit produces 
important changes in the CeN physical properties. In particular, the Ce–N coordination decreases 
from sixfold to threefold, accompanied by a significant shortening of the Ce –N bonds and the 
formation of an essentially planar hexagonal lattice. Dimensional reduction also modifies the 
electronic and magnetic behavior, allowing well -defined FM and AFM configurations with 
magnetic moments predominantly localized on the Ce atoms and mainly associated with the Ce 4f 
states. The FM configuration is slightly lower in energy than the AFM state, indicating a close 
energetic competition between different magnetic arrangements in the monolayer. 
 
Interestingly, despite the clear influence of magnetic ordering on the electronic and magnetic 
properties, the underlying structural and mechanical characteristics are only weakly affected by 
the orientation of the magnetic moments. The FM and AFM configurations exhibit nearly identical 
equilibrium geometries, Ce–N bond lengths, elastic responses, and phonon spectra, indicating that 

these properties are governed predominantly by the Ce –N bonding network rather than by the 
specific magnetic arrangement. The elastic, phonon, and ab initio molecular dynamics results 
further support the mechanical, dynamical, and finite-temperature stability of the two-dimensional 
structure. Overall, our results show that dimensional reduction has a much stronger influence on 
the physical properties of CeN than the change between FM and AFM magnetic ordering, while 
the structural and mechanical framework r emain remarkably robust against changes in the 
magnetic configuration. The coexistence of structural stability, localized Ce  4f magnetism, and 
spin-dependent electronic properties make the two-dimensional CeN as a novel interesting system 
for further investigations of magnetic 2D materials and potential spin -dependent and spintronic 
applications.

This paper introduced the Concept Lifecycle Model (CLM), which formalises concepts as persistent, graph-grounded, temporally versioned entities with explicit provenance and epistemic status, and Concept-Grounded Attention (CGA), which incorporates concept-graph information into transformer computation through graph-biased self-attention (Form A) and gated cross-attention over concept nodes (Form B). The failure of Form B was caused by a normalisation that did not preserve the pretrained computation; a repaired Form B improved answers, but mostly through added trainable capacity, as concepts from other questions produced most of the same gain; a borderline concept-specific gain with a strong relevance prior did not replicate with a larger model, and a query-conditioned Form A gained no more than a shuffled control. Representing time improved temporal question answering for every generator tested, by 13 to 25 points and most strongly for the largest models, but simplified CLM version resolution did not outperform dated serialisation, because concept identity was not established reliably. Protocol-derived epistemic status nearly eliminated unsupported assertions in a controlled setting where source independence must be judged, and models of 72 to 122 billion parameters that were told the rule could not replace it, still asserting unconfirmed claims in 19 to 68 percent of cases.






Taken together, the findings support the representational premises of the CLM, that temporal validity and epistemic status should be explicit, more than they support the proposed mechanisms for injecting graph structure into attention. title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
hypothesis:
Once design is placed beyond the institution’s reach, the question stops being which fairness method performs best and becomes what fairness work is even possible, and for whom. The ASP-HEI cycle (Section 
2
) predicts that adopting algorithms under these conditions will deepen existing inequities and concentrate institutional power 
(
McConvey and Guha, 2024
)
; we test whether the post-hoc methods the literature recommends for constrained settings can interrupt that pattern or whether they reproduce it. This paper examines what fairness work is possible within the narrow intervention space this arrangement creates. This study examines one concrete governance site within this cycle: the moment when an institution, already locked into a vendor-controlled predictive system, attempts to enact fairness on outputs it can observe but cannot meaningfully interrogate.
conclusion:
7. 
Conclusion




Using a held-out test set of 42,138 student records drawn from a 168,550-record modeling cohort, we stress-tested six post-hoc fairness interventions under the constraints procurement actually imposes. No method delivered consistent equity gains. Improvements for one group came with new gaps for another, well-represented students benefited most, and marginalized ones stayed disadvantaged. Beyond these expected trade-offs, we found three patterns that should trouble anyone deploying these methods: an implementation can operationalize disadvantage in a way that contradicts observed disparities, as two of ours did for residency; a single constraint that corrects reasonably for one attribute can fail catastrophically for another; and an implementation choice invisible to the institution can decide whether a method helps, does nothing, or does harm.
These are not independent obstacles. They are linked stages of the same structural dynamic 
(
McConvey and Guha, 2024
)
: financial pressures produce the vendor dependencies that foreclose real intervention, the scarce advising capacity that makes parity-seeking methods unworkable, and the data practices that render students at the margins invisible. A post-hoc method acting at a single downstream point of that cycle cannot reach the conditions that generate the disparities it is asked to correct. Fairness, on this account, is not a one-time optimization but ongoing work of negotiation and judgment, distributed across actors with deeply unequal power to carry it out.
This is where our contribution to CSCW sits. We reframe post-hoc fairness in procured AI as a problem of cooperative work rather than a property of a model; we introduce error-type profiling to translate fairness metrics into the caseloads advisors actually manage; and we document fairness theatre empirically, showing how adjustments can satisfy dashboard metrics while the burdens students carry stay put or grow. Prior work theorized how algorithm adoption consolidates institutional power 
(
McConvey and Guha, 2024
)
. Our findings show that fairness interventions, confined to the narrow space vendor control permits, can become instruments of that consolidation rather than checks on it. Closing the gap will take more than better tools. It will take governance that reclaims oversight of algorithmic design, aligns institutional capacity with the support students need, and refuses to accept the appearance of fairness in place of its substance.

explicit directional information into the signal channel is insufficient to restore the behavior obtained in 2D. Achieving 
full functional transfer may require the receiving agent to re-evolve its navigational capabilities in a 3D environment.

coordinated behavior supported by that mechanism. These findings suggest partial re-evolution and latent-space world 
models as potential strategies for achieving robust transfer of coevolved coordination between two-dimensional and
